TOPIC 1: DNA STRUCTURE & REPLICATION

The “Transforming Principle” 
In 1928, an experiment was conducted by Frederick Griffith which demonstrated that bacteria can be re-programmed through a process called transformation… 
Griffith’s experiment suggested that something inside the cell must be responsible for its programming, and that this molecule could be transferred from cell to cell.
The molecule that was responsible for the cell’s programming (aka the hereditary material) was still up for debate… 
Note: We have to know some names of scientists and their contributions to our understanding of genetics and heredity. (i.e. testable)

A Case for DNA as the “Transforming Principle” 
In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase conducted a series of experiments to prove that DNA, and not protein, was the hereditary material.
This involved radio-labelling the proteins and DNA associated with a particular virus and allowing it to infect a bacterium to see which factor would be “injected” to transform the bacterium.
The Hershey-Chase Experiment:

DNA: The Hereditary Material
DNA is the nucleic acid molecule that governs the processes of heredity in all plant and animal cells. 
Every cell in your body (with the exception of your gametes) contains the same DNA within its nucleus
The way that DNA is expressed, however, differs from cell to cell
I.e. not every gene is turned on in every cell

The DNA Nucleotide
Dna is made up of long chains of individual units (monomers) called nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of:

A five-carbon sugar
A phosphate group
One of four nitrogenous bases: 
Adenine (A) 
Guanine (G)
Cytosine (C)
Thymine (T)


Purines have a double ring (adenine and guanine), whereas pyrimidines have a single ring (thymine and cytosine)


More on uracil later

The Structure of DNA

DNA molecules form a double helix, with a sugar-phosphate backbone held together by complementary nitrogenous base pairs. The “rules” for each DNA molecule include… 
Hydrogen bonds form between nitrogenous base pairs
Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T)
Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G)
Each base is bonded to a sugar group.
Sugar groups are bonded to phosphates.
The grouping that exists between a phosphate molecule, a sugar molecule, and a single nitrogenous base is collectively referred to as a nucleotide



NUCLEOTIDE

The Structure of DNA
DNA strands are also said to be antiparallel, meaning that they run in the opposite direction as one another:
The 5’ and 3’ ends run in opposite directions
These numbers come from organic chemistry naming rules, and simply describe a particular carbon in the sugar, and thus the orientation of the nucleotide
This property has important implications for DNA replication & protein synthesis

But how did we come to know so much about the structure of DNA?
This became known as Chargaff’s Rule. 
The AT:GC ratio is same for same species and different for different species
The amount of A = the amount of T
The amount of C = the amount of G
A+T does not necessarily equal G+C

	
	

In the 1940s, Erwin Chargaff figured out that the 4 different nitrogenous bases aren’t present in equal amounts. They are present in varied, yet characteristic proportions where A=T and C=G.

More reading if interested:
https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/james-watson-francis-crick-maurice-wilkins-and-rosalind-franklin

Discovering the Structure of DNA:
In the 1950s, British scientist Rosalind Franklin used X-ray photography to analyze the structure of DNA. Her observations provided crucial new information about the molecular structure of DNA. 
In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick were the first to produce the structural model of DNA that could account for all the evidence from Franklin’s experiments as well as Chargaff’s observations.
Re-cap: The DNA Molecule

DNA Replication 
During S phase of interphase, a cell replicates its entire genome in order to produce a new cell with an identical set of DNA. 
Each strand of DNA serves as a template for the creation of its complementary strand
DNA replication is thus said to be semi-conservative; that is, each new molecule of DNA contains one strand of the original DNA molecule and one newly synthesized strand

The Meselson-Stahl Experiment
The semiconservative nature of DNA replication was proven by the Meselson-Stahl Experiment.
The semiconservative model maintains that the original double helix serves as a template for, but does not contribute to, a new double helix.
The Meselson-Stahl Experiment

DNA Replication
Watch these videos first, then read the summary in the next slides. You may then come back and re-watch these videos, or find others to better understand the process as a whole.

STEP 1: INITIATION
A group of enzymes known as helicases bind to a specific sequence of DNA referred to as the replication origin
The helicases then “cut” and unravel the double helix. The y-shaped area that forms where the DNA is split is known as the replication fork, while the unwound region is known as the replication bubble.
The single unwound strands of DNA serve as templates for replication

DNA Replication

STEP 2: ELONGATION
A primer sequence synthesized by the RNA primase enzyme signals DNA polymerase where to begin.
DNA polymerase begins to add nucleotides within the replication bubble, creating two new strands of DNA that are complementary to each existing strand.
Once replication is complete, the primers are removed by DNA polymerase 
Elongation always takes place in the 5’ to 3’ direction, meaning that one strand will always be “leading” (replicated continuously) and the other will always be “lagging” (replicated in short segments known as Okazaki fragments)
Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand are spliced (‘glued’) together by an enzyme known as DNA ligase


Tip: There’s often meaning in words in biology. Anything that ends in ‘ase’ is an enzyme, that ‘makes something happen’. A polymer, is a long chain of monomer subunits, such as nucleotides. DNA polymerase, therefore is an enzyme that creates DNA polymerase.

STEP 3: TERMINATION
As soon as the newly formed strands are complete, they rewind automatically into their chemically stable helix structure
Replication proceeds until the two new DNA molecules separate; the dismantling of the replication complex is known as termination

Key Enzymes to Know
ENZYME
FUNCTION
helicase
Cleaves (cuts) and unwinds DNA 
RNA primase
Synthesizes primer to begin elongation process
DNA polymerase
adds new nucleotides from 5’ end to 3’ end of existing strand and removes primer sequences from DNA once replication is complete
DNA ligase
Splices together Okazaki fragments of lagging strand

TOPIC 2: TRANSCRIPTION & TRANSLATION

Recall that DNA provides the “instructions” for each of our cells.
Each segment of DNA (gene) is responsible for encoding a specific protein, which carries out a specific function.
Not every gene is expressed in each cell. This is what allows cells to specialize and function differently. 
Some genes do not appear to code for any proteins… “junk” DNA? 


Gene Expression

Central Dogma of Biology
In order for a segment of DNA to be expressed by a cell, it must first be transcribed into mRNA (messenger RNA) and then translated into a sequence of amino acids (a protein). This is referred to as the “central dogma” of gene expression.
Allows different cells to express different genes
So, although all cells contain the same DNA, not all cells behave the same
Okay, so what is RNA exactly?

From DNA to Protein
Again, watch these videos first, then read the summary in the next slides. You may then come back and re-watch these videos, or find others to better understand the process as a whole.

Transcription 
During transcription, the information in a segment of double-stranded DNA is copied into a single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA) 
Transcription takes place within the nucleus of a cell.
Only one strand of the DNA (the coding or “sense” strand) is transcribed into mRNA. SInce only one strand is transcribed, there is no need for Okazaki fragments here. 
The other strand is referred to as non-coding or antisense strand. 
Transcription is initiated when RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region of the coding strand and begins to add complementary base pairs in the 5’ to 3’ direction.
Whenever a thymine should be inserted, it is replaced by uracil (U’s instead of T’s) because in RNA, there is no thymine.
Once RNA polymerase reaches a termination sequence, the mRNA strand is complete and can leave the nucleus to be translated into a protein.
Transcription

Before translation takes place, the mRNA sequence is modified to remove sequences of mRNA called introns.
Introns are sequences of RNA that do not code for proteins.
The remaining RNA sequences are referred to as exons. 
This modification process occurs only in eukaryotes.

Extra: mRNA processing

2)  Translation
Once DNA is transcribed into mRNA, it then leaves the nucleus and moves into the cytoplasm of the cell to be translated into a protein.
The mRNA sequence is split into codons (groups of three base pairs), each of which links to a specific amino acid through the use of transfer RNA (tRNA).
Codons are linked to amino acids by tRNA anticodons.
Ribosomes (ribosomal RNA - rRNA) serve as the functional units of protein synthesis, working with tRNA to translate mRNA into amino acids

Ribosomes are typically free-floating within the cytoplasm; these ribosomes produce proteins for use within the cell.
Ribosomes consist of two subunits: a large subunit and a small subunit. The mRNA sequence is “sandwiched” between these two subunits when it is translated.
Each codon to be translated arrives at the “A” site of the ribosome with the help of tRNA. It then moves to the “P” site, where the correct amino acid is attached to the growing polypeptide chain. It then exits at the “E” site.
Bound ribosomes produce proteins for export.

Table of mRNA codons (in your data booklet) and corresponding amino acids
For example, if the mRNA sequence is AGC, the amino acid ‘serine’ will be inserted during translation
Remember!! You must be using mRNA to look up the amino acid in this table. 
AUG - is an initiator or start codon. The ribosomes will ‘scan’ the mRNA sequence, and only begin translating at AUG. AUG therefore also set the reading frame for the mRNA.

UAA, UAG, and UGA - terminator or stop codons. The ribosome will stop translating here and the protein in finished. 
Codons to Amino Acids

A closer look at tRNA
E.g. a tRNA with an anticodon of CGG, will carry alanine, because the complementary mRNA codon is GCC. REMEMBER: You have to look up mRNA in your data booklet.
Although tRNA is still single stranded, like other RNA molecules, it also has a looped structure. 
We don’t need to worry too much about the loops, but one of its loops contains the anticodon, through which the tRNA molecule binds to the complementary codon in the mRNA molecule.

How many nucleotides are required to code for the following sequence of amino acids?

Is it possible to determine the mRNA sequence that is responsible for producing the sequence of amino acids above? Explain…
No. More than one codon codes for most AAs. For example, leucine can come from an mRNA sequence of UUA, UUG, or anything that begins with CU_



15 nucleotide (each AA requires a codon, which is a nucleotide triplet

The previous practice question illustrates the redundancy of the genetic code. This means that most amino acids are encoded for by different mRNA codons, and therefore different DNA nucleotide triples.
But no codon will ever specify for two different amino acids
Redundancy is a good thing, when we consider mutations.  For example, if the normal DNA sequence is CAA, but during DNA replication DNA polymerase inserts a G instead of the second A and now the DNA sequence is CAG, it still codes for glutamine. The finished protein will be no different.

TOPIC 3: MUTATIONS AND GENETIC TECHNOLOGIES

Mutations
Mistakes in the coding of genetic information often take place during DNA replication, transcription and/or translation. Most of the mistakes get corrected right away, by various proofing mechanisms cells have. Mistakes that do not get corrected, however, result in the production of a different sequence than what was intended. These mistakes are referred to as mutations. Certain types of mutations have more severe consequences than others. 
Mutations that occur in somatic cells (body cells) are not passed on to offspring (e.g. cancer)
Mutations that occur in the germ line (reproductive cells) are passed on to offspring (e.g.  trisomy 21)

Types of Mutations
POINT MUTATION

Chemical change that affects just one nucleotide
This involves the substitution of one nucleotide for another (e.g. a “G” instead of an “A”)
Point mutations can be
silent: no change in AA
missense: change to new AA
nonsense: change to stop codon

An insertion or deletion of a nucleotide that causes the entire reading frame of the gene to be altered
Typically has more severe consequences, as it changes the protein entirely (not just a single amino acid)

Mutations & Natural Selection
Mutations Summary

Mitochondrial DNA
By analyzing the mtDNA of a species, we can actually trace back lineages through time to identify a common ancestor	
mtDNA mutations usually aren’t lethal, so mutations can accumulate in great numbers over time
mtDNA is also shorter, which makes sequencing easier
The more similar mtDNA sequences, the more closely related organisms are

DNA is not just found in the nucleus of the cell; it is also stored in the mitochondria. However, unlike nuclear DNA, mtDNA is only inherited from the mother. This is because all cytoplasm and organelles, such as mitochondria, come from the egg; sperm just contributes DNA. 
According to our most current understanding, some mitochondria may be donated by the sperm and therefore mtDNA can be paternal, but this is much less frequent and we will ignore for Bio 30.

Why do mitochondria contain DNA?
Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) have their own DNA, because they used to be their own free living bacteria. Through the process of endosymbiosis they came to be part of eukaryotic cells.

Genetic Engineering
A molecule of DNA that includes genetic material from different sources is called recombinant DNA. It is produced through the process of genetic engineering. 
Genetic engineering is used globally to produce organisms with desirable traits that could not be produced via selective breeding (Genetically Modified Organisms - GMOs). 
E.g. herbicide resistant canola or corn
E.g. mass-production of human insulin by bacteria.
Genetic engineering often involves taking plasmids from bacteria (circular segments of DNA which contain their genetic info) and re-programming them to express certain genes. 
Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) “cut” the DNA sequence at a specific recognition site to allow for the insertion of a desired gene, which is “glued” into the genome using DNA ligase.

General steps involved with genetic engineering and creating insulin producing bacteria:
Use restriction enzymes to cut and remove functioning insulin gene from a human pancreatic cell
Use the same restriction enzyme on a plasmid to get same ‘sticky ends’. These are usually palindromic sequences.

Genetic engineering is a fast growing field of science. There are so many fascinating and instructional videos on the internet. I encourage you to seek out some videos on this topic to learn more. Here are a few to get started with:

Gel Electrophoresis
Through a process known as gel electrophoresis, we can analyze and compare the DNA of any organism:
Involves applying a current to a gel made of agarose sugar → there is a positive electrode end and a negative electrode end

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific points, forming a series of varying sized fragments
DNA is negatively charged, so it will migrate towards the positive electrode
The smaller the fragment, the easier it is to move through the gel, therefore smaller fragments will migrate further
The banding pattern of the gel allows us to compare samples of DNA
E.g. Samples #1 and #4 display the same banding pattern, indicating that the organisms they were taken from are closely related, most likely being the same individual
